message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What You’re Generally Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|-----------------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written record of the deposit amount and any receipts.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds money. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.).
• Must comply with all applicable building, health, and safety codes. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy (pay for repairs yourself and deduct from rent, but only under specific circumstances). | | **Rent Payment & Late Fees** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Landlords may charge a late fee, but it must be reasonable and disclosed in the lease. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment, excessive noise, or unlawful entry. | | **Entry by Landlord** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries; if the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, obtain a judgment, and then obtain a writ of possession. | • Respond to notices promptly; if you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a counter‑claim or seek a stay of execution. | | **Privacy & Personal Property** | • Landlord cannot seize or damage your personal property without a court order. | • Keep a list of your belongings; report any theft or damage immediately. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities unless otherwise stated in the lease. | • Verify which utilities are your responsibility; dispute any unauthorized charges. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s consent. | • Obtain written permission; keep a copy of the sublease agreement. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can:
1. File a complaint with TDHCA or HUD/TCHR.
2. Seek a small‑claims judgment (up to $20,000).
3. File a civil suit for damages. | • Keep all documentation (emails, texts, repair receipts, photos). | ### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Look for clauses on security deposits, maintenance responsibilities, pet policies, and notice periods. 2. **Ask About Repairs** – Confirm who pays for what (e.g., HVAC, plumbing). 3. **Document the Condition** – Take photos or videos of the unit before you move in. 4. **Get Everything in Writing** – Oral agreements are hard to enforce. ### Resources - **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** – [https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us](https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us) - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – [https://www.hud.gov](https://www.hud.gov) - **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** – [https://www.tchr.texas.gov](https://www.tchr.texas.gov) - **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** – e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local bar associations. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a habitable home, proper notice for entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for disputes and evictions. Keep thorough records, communicate in writing, and use the above resources if you encounter problems.
